headline: New moon springs load up the flood at Kings Point as bass and blues stack on bunker
subhead: Building tides and a warming Sound are pushing fish onto the rockpiles at Execution and Stepping Stones — here's where to be for the evening flood.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound settled into that mid-summer rhythm where the tides do more talking than the wind. We had a stretch of light southwest breeze, nothing that churned things up, and the harbor water crept warmer day over day — Manhasset and Hempstead are running full summer temps now, the kind of water that pushes bait tight to structure and makes fish work the edges instead of roaming open water. The moon's been waning down toward new, which means the tidal range has been building all week, and by the time you read this we're heading into new-moon springs peaking around July 11-13. That's the tide I've been waiting for. Bigger swings mean more water moving through the pinch points — Throgs Neck, the Stepping Stones light, the gut off Hart Island — and more water moving means bait gets pushed, stripers get aggressive, and the bite windows get longer.

Here's the piece that matters most this week: that new-moon flood is stacking up right at sunset at Kings Point. We haven't had a PM flood-sunset window line up like this since the June full moon, and when the high stand and last light converge, Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones corridor turn into a highway. I'd be positioning by 7:30 PM through dark, working the last two hours of the incoming. This is not a subtle bite when it's on — but I want to be straight with you, it's been feast or famine the last ten days depending on whether the bunker schools cooperate, so don't burn your whole trip on one spot if the first hour is dead.

Speaking of bunker — Matinecock Point has been holding pods since mid-June and they're still there, thick enough that you can see them nervous-watering off the point on a calm morning. That's your tell. When those bunker get pushed and start skipping on the surface, there are stripers and blues underneath working them from below. I've had the best luck snagging a bunker on a weighted treble and free-lining it back into the school, no weight, just let it swim naturally into the chaos. Bass in the 28 to 36-inch range have been coming off that pattern, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in — I heard of quality fish showing up in pockets around the Sound and further east this year, and Matinecock's been one of the places holding its share of them. If you don't want to snag bait, a big white Savage Gear or Tsunami swim shad, 6 to 8 inches, worked slow through the edge of the school does the job too.

Execution Rocks is fishing true to form on the outgoing — that's been the pattern here for thirty years and it hasn't changed. Start right as the tide turns and work bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounce white or chartreuse with a white Fin-S trailer, bounced along the rockpile in 15 to 25 feet. Blues have been mixed in with the bass out there, choppers in the 3 to 6-pound class, and they'll murder a bucktail just as fast as a bass will, so bring extra rigs because you will get bit off.

Fluke has been the trickier story this year. The bay-side water in the back harbors got warm fast — warmer than fluke like to sit in for long — and that's pushed the better fish out toward the channel edges and the deeper cuts near the bridges. I'm finding them now stacked along the Throgs Neck Bridge rips and the deeper drop-offs off Willets Point, 25 to 35 feet, drifting 4-inch white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and tight to bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. It's not been an easy pick — you're covering water and culling through shorts to find a keeper — but the ones we are getting have been quality, three to four pounds, with the occasional five.

Porgies are exactly where they should be in July — thick on the rockpiles at Stepping Stones and around Execution, and this is about as reliable a bite as we get all season. Bloodworms or clam on a high-low rig, light sinker, right in the boulders in 20 to 30 feet on the last of the incoming through the top of the tide. Easy limits for anyone willing to anchor up and be patient.

Blackfish are quiet right now, which is normal — this isn't their season and I wouldn't waste a trip on them until the water starts cooling in September. And I have to be honest about weakfish: I haven't heard a real report out of this zone in weeks. The water's been warm enough on paper, but that species has been a ghost for us this summer, and I'm not going to sell you a pattern that isn't there. If you're set on weakfish, work the inlets on a clean outgoing at first light with bucktails and grubs, but don't build a trip around it.

Looking ahead — if that new-moon spring tide holds through the weekend like the setup suggests, Sunday and Monday evenings at Kings Point are where I'd put my time. Bring bunker gear and bucktails both, because you won't know which bite is on until you're out there watching the surface. Plan B if the bunker scatter: drop back to Execution on the outgoing and work the bottom instead of the top. Either way, the tide's finally doing us a favor this week — don't waste it.
